title: Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen (June 2022 TCC) Ruling
subject: Technological Uncertainty Is Judged Objectively Against a Competent Professional
keyPhrase: Daves Diesel v The Queen 2022 TCC
summary: In Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen (2022 TCC 62), the Tax Court of Canada dismissed a Brampton, Ontario diesel fuel injection firm's SR&ED appeals for its 2013 and 2014 taxation years. The key takeaway for Canadian claimants: technological uncertainty is judged objectively against a competent professional, and claims need discrete hypotheses, systematic experimentation and contemporaneous records.
metaDescription: Review the June 2022 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen and its impact on Canadian R&D claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

On June 10, 2022, the Tax Court of Canada issued its judgment in Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen (2022 TCC 62, Docket: 2018-1618(IT)G), following a General Procedure hearing in Hamilton, Ontario, on May 10, 2022. Presided over by the Honourable Justice David E. Spiro, the appeal addressed a fundamental tension in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive law: the distinction between subjective commercial self-teaching through reverse engineering and objective technological experimentation conducted in accordance with the scientific method. The Court ultimately dismissed the taxpayer's appeals for the 2013 and 2014 taxation years in their entirety, awarding costs to the Crown in accordance with the Tariff.
Commercial Context and the Taxpayer's Claim

The Appellant, Dave's Diesel Inc., operated a diesel fuel injection service facility in Brampton, Ontario, founded by the father of the company's General Manager, Mr. Rushi Dave, approximately a decade prior to the disputed project. Historically, the Appellant's business model relied on original equipment manufacturer (OEM) warranty programs for mechanical diesel fuel injection systems. Under these arrangements, the Appellant received defective mechanical fuel injection components from engine shops and dealerships, disassembled the units, assessed failure modes, replaced worn parts with brand-new components, and recalibrated the reassembled injectors on a test stand to meet manufacturer specifications.

By 2007 or 2008, a structural shift had begun in the diesel engine industry as electronic fuel injection systems began to replace legacy mechanical systems. Concurrently, manufacturers would no longer pay the Appellant to remanufacture components of their used fuel injection systems under their warranty programs. Facing a severe contraction in its core revenue stream, the Appellant sought to pivot its business model toward independently remanufacturing used electronic and mechanical fuel injectors—using discarded injectors as "cores"—to sell to end-users, resellers, and engine rebuilders at price points below OEM list prices for new units.

During its 2013 and 2014 taxation years, the Appellant claimed to have undertaken an experimental development project aimed at establishing a proprietary remanufacturing procedure for three specific fuel injector models: the Delphi 4 Pin, the Caterpillar C7, and the Cummins ISX. Across all three injector platforms, the Appellant executed a standardized four-step workflow. In the first step, the Appellant disassembled the used fuel injector without fracturing or destroying its internal components, which included fabricating custom disassembly tools simply to understand the internal mechanics of the unit. The second step involved placing the injector in one of the Appellant's machines to simulate its operation and ascertain which of its parts were likely to fail. In the third step, the workers sourced or modified replacement components intended to rectify or improve upon those failure points. Finally, the fourth step consisted of reassembling the remanufactured injectors and testing them to meet or exceed original manufacturer specifications.

For the 2013 taxation year, the Appellant claimed SR&ED expenditures of $56,065 and deducted SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) of $26,865, claimed under a combination of subsection 127(5), subsection 127(9), and subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act"). For the 2014 taxation year, the Appellant claimed SR&ED expenditures of $69,604 and ITCs of $31,134. Notably, the evidentiary record established at trial revealed that the Appellant did not actually complete the remanufacturing of any of the three types of fuel injectors during either the 2013 or 2014 taxation years.
The Minister's Challenge and the Governing Statutory Framework

The Minister of National Revenue (through the Canada Revenue Agency [CRA]) assessed the Appellant to disallow the deduction of the claimed ITCs, together with the claimed SR&ED expenditures, for both taxation years. The Crown contended that the work performed by the Appellant's personnel—composed entirely of Mr. Rushi Dave, his father, and two unskilled labourers whom the Appellant said it had trained (although the Court noted it was never made clear exactly what training was given)—did not constitute "experimental development" within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Act.

The statutory authority governing SR&ED claims in Canada is anchored in subsection 248(1) of the Act, which defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statutory definition divides eligible activities into four distinct categories. Paragraph (a) covers basic research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Paragraph (b) encompasses applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph (c)—the focal provision in commercial industrial claims—governs experimental development, which is work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Finally, paragraph (d) captures support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c).

To determine whether the Appellant's activities satisfied paragraph (c) of subsection 248(1), Justice Spiro applied the canonical five-question judicial test formulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC). Justice Spiro explicitly noted that the Federal Court of Appeal had endorsed, on several occasions, the five criteria of the Northwest Hydraulic framework, most recently in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47 and following Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88), where Justice Rennie confirmed that the five criteria reflect the judiciary's settled interpretation of Parliament's intent in enacting subsection 248(1). Under this framework, a claimant must establish on a balance of probabilities that five cumulative conditions are satisfied. First, there must have been a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the person claiming to be doing SR&ED must have formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the procedures adopted must have accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the process must have resulted in a technological advance. Fifth, although the Income Tax Act and its Regulations do not expressly mandate the form of records, a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results must have been kept as the work progressed.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice Spiro held that the Appellant failed to satisfy a single criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic test. The Court determined that the Appellant improperly relied on the subjective ignorance of non-engineers and non-mechanics to allege technological uncertainty, conflated its overarching commercial objective with a scientific hypothesis, engaged in unrecorded trial-and-error tinkering rather than systematic experimentation, and failed to demonstrate any technological advancement. Because the Appellant failed to discharge its evidentiary onus on a balance of probabilities under subsection 248(1), the appeals for the 2013 and 2014 taxation years were dismissed with costs.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of the SR&ED claims in Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen provides an exhaustive blueprint of the legal, technical, and evidentiary vulnerabilities that frequently undermine Canadian small-to-medium enterprise (SME) tax credit filings. Justice Spiro's analysis systematically dismantled the Appellant's position across five primary legal and evidentiary axes.
The Objective Standard of Technological Uncertainty and the Competent Professional Baseline

The foundational threshold of any experimental development claim under paragraph 248(1)(c) is the existence of a "technological risk or uncertainty" that cannot be resolved through "routine engineering or standard procedures". In Canadian tax jurisprudence, "routine engineering" is legally defined as those techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant field of science or technology. Consequently, technological uncertainty arises only when a project's objective is obstructed by a technical limitation or system conflict that a professional possessing the requisite academic qualifications, training, and industry expertise could not resolve without resorting to hypothesis-driven experimentation.

In Dave's Diesel, the Appellant's case collapsed at this threshold due to a profound evidentiary gap regarding personnel qualifications and the state of the art. During the 2013 and 2014 taxation years, only four individuals worked on the injector project: Mr. Rushi Dave (General Manager), his father, and two unskilled labourers whom the Appellant said it had trained, although exactly what training was given was never made clear. The evidence established that Mr. Dave did not study mechanical engineering and held no degree, certificate, or designation in that field; rather, his academic background was in business and marketing, and he had worked for a large advertising, marketing, and public relations firm before joining the family business 15 years before the hearing. Furthermore, although Mr. Dave characterized the Appellant as a diesel fuel injection shop, the Court found that it was not a mechanic shop, as no mechanics worked there, and that none of the individuals involved in the project in 2013 or 2014 were engineers or mechanics.

As described in the Court's reasons, Step 1 of its four-step process consisted of disassembling the Delphi 4 Pin, C7, and ISX injectors simply because the Appellant "did not understand how the injectors worked, so it needed to take them apart first". Because none of the four workers were engineers or mechanics, every aspect of the project appeared to them to be a "technological uncertainty".
Justice Spiro rejected this subjective framing in stark terms, emphasizing that the legal standard for technological uncertainty under subsection 248(1) is strictly objective:

"The Appellant rests its case on the subjective knowledge of the four non-engineers and non-mechanics who worked on the project. To them, every aspect of the project was a 'technological uncertainty'. The 'technological uncertainty' standard, however, is not subjective. If it were subjective, a grade school student trying to build a simple electric motor would meet the test."

Reinforcing this principle, Justice Spiro cited the jurisprudence of Justice Monaghan (when she was a member of the Tax Court of Canada) in Logix Data Products Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 36, at paragraph 69), establishing that technological uncertainty "does not arise simply because the Appellant does not have the requisite knowledge". Rather, the lacking knowledge must genuinely be absent from the established base of scientific or technological knowledge, and the determinative legal question is "whether the uncertainty identified by the Appellant is an uncertainty to those knowledgeable and experienced in the relevant field". The burden rested entirely on Dave's Diesel Inc. to prove, through credible technical evidence or expert testimony, that a competent professional in the field—a mechanical engineer, for example, or, as the Court noted, potentially a knowledgeable and experienced diesel engine mechanic—could not have remanufactured the used fuel injectors using routine engineering and standard procedures. By failing to adduce any evidence benchmarking its difficulties against the capabilities of a competent professional in the field (the Appellant called neither a mechanical engineer nor a duly qualified diesel engine mechanic, and there was no evidence that taking a fuel injector apart without breaking it, or understanding how it worked, was anything other than routine engineering or standard procedure for such a professional), the Appellant failed the first Northwest Hydraulic criterion.
The Conflation of Commercial Objectives with Discrete Scientific Hypotheses

The second criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic test requires the taxpayer to formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the identified technological uncertainty. As articulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic, the formulation of hypotheses sits within a structured five-stage progression of the scientific method. This systematic methodology begins with the observation of the subject matter of the problem, proceeds to the formulation of a clear objective, moves to the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, advances to the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate that uncertainty, and culminates in the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

At trial, when asked to identify the technological uncertainty faced by the company, Mr. Dave testified that the uncertainty was "whether we could successfully develop a process to remanufacture the injector[s]". Subsequently, when asked to state the scientific hypothesis formulated by the team, Mr. Dave testified that the hypothesis was "whether we could develop a remanufacturing procedure and be able to remanufacture these injectors, and that's the hypothesis".
Justice Spiro dismantled this circular testimony, observing:
"Only in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland could it be argued that one's hypothesis is the 'technological uncertainty' and that the 'technological uncertainty' is one's hypothesis."

This judicial rebuke highlights a pervasive error in unsuccessful SR&ED claims: the conflation of a high-level commercial or project objective with both the technological uncertainty and the testable hypothesis. Citing Justice Sommerfeldt's analysis in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6, at paragraph 26), which in turn cited Advanced Agricultural Testing Inc. v. The Queen (2009 TCC 190 at paragraphs 30–31), Justice Spiro reiterated that a hypothesis is legally and scientifically defined as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial".

The Northwest Hydraulic standard does not contemplate a single, overarching meta-question ("Can we build this product or process?") governing a multi-year commercial effort. Instead, the statutory scheme requires discrete, falsifiable hypotheses that precede each individual experimental trial, specify causal relationships between technical variables, and undergo iterative modification in light of empirical test results.

To provide a clear pedagogical benchmark for practitioners and taxpayers, Justice Spiro examined an entry from Mr. Dave's handwritten diary dated February 25, 2013, which read: "Received prototype [C7 adapter] from machine shop and installed. The thinner O-ring would not stand up to the pressure and kept breaking." Justice Spiro explained that the hypothesis to be tested in respect of this entry might have been the following, and that it would have been the subject of the test, with the results recorded and analyzed and the hypothesis modified in light of them:
"An O-ring 5 mm. thick should withstand pressure of 50 lb/ft. as effectively as an O-ring 7.5 mm. thick."

Under a compliant SR&ED protocol, that specific predictive statement would be formulated prior to testing, subjected to controlled pressurization, measured quantitatively, analyzed upon failure, and systematically modified for the next experimental iteration. In Dave's Diesel, the Appellant could not point to a single test conducted in 2013 or 2014 where a discrete hypothesis was formulated prior to testing, tested systematically, and modified based on the resulting data.
Departure from the Scientific Method: Simple Trial and Error Versus Systematic Experimentation

The third Northwest Hydraulic requirement mandates that the procedures adopted by the taxpayer accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment. In Footnote 17 of the judgment, Justice Spiro explicitly defined "simple trial and error" as "testing without the prior formulation of a hypothesis".

During the hearing, the Appellant produced physical exhibits consisting of one fully assembled and one disassembled fuel injector for each of the three models (Exhibits AP-1 to AP-6), alongside concise handwritten notebook entries documenting shop floor activities. While Mr. Dave explained minor structural differences among the Delphi 4 Pin, C7, and ISX injectors, Justice Spiro found those mechanical differences immaterial because the Appellant applied the exact same unscientific methodology to all three.

The diary entries revealed, among other things, that the workers broke a Delphi 4 Pin injector while trying to understand how it came apart, used a thin steel punch to pop out a terminal insulating sleeve and seal, ran trials with different shim thicknesses, and conducted spring pressure trials. Justice Spiro concluded that even a cursory review of these entries suggested the project had more in common with empirical "tinkering" and "simple trial and error" than with the scientific method, and that there was no evidence any of the four individuals used established and objective principles of scientific method. The fatal deficiency in the Appellant's testing regime was the complete absence of controlled variables, baseline standards, and quantitative metrology. Addressing the Appellant's alleged "spring pressure tests" and "shim thickness tests," Justice Spiro posed, in his analysis of the fifth criterion, a series of evidentiary questions to which there was no record of the answers. Specifically, the Court inquired as to what quantitative standard was selected for passing the test, what exact pressures were applied and for what durations during the spring pressure tests, what empirical results were recorded for each test at each pressure and duration, and at what precise pressure threshold and point each spring failed.

Because the Appellant failed to establish baseline parameters, control variables, or record quantitative failure points, its shop-floor adjustments lacked the methodical rigour required by the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), where Justice Rennie upheld the Tax Court's finding that the taxpayer's records were "vague," "unclear," and did not reflect "a logical progression between the premise of an experiment and the result".
Mischaracterization of Technological Advancement

Under the fourth Northwest Hydraulic question and the express language of paragraph 248(1)(c), experimental development must be undertaken for the purpose of achieving a "technological advancement". Even where a project fails to achieve its ultimate commercial performance targets, it must generate new technological knowledge that advances the baseline understanding of competent professionals in the field.

In evaluating what the Appellant's project actually sought to achieve, Justice Spiro drew a sharp legal distinction between commercial or social utility and technological advancement. The Court acknowledged that successfully remanufacturing discarded diesel fuel injectors rather than disposing of them in landfills might represent an "environmental advance". Similarly, developing an in-house capability to rebuild used injector cores to replace lost OEM warranty revenue might have resulted in a "financial advance" for the Appellant's business. However, neither environmental sustainability nor corporate profitability equates to a "technological advance" within the meaning of the Income Tax Act.

Although the record showed that the Appellant was attempting to remanufacture used injectors by disassembling them and replacing parts likely to fail—and that it did not remanufacture any of the three types of injectors during its 2013 or 2014 taxation years—Justice Spiro's finding on this criterion rested on the absence of evidence of any technological advance, as he stated: "But, after hearing all the evidence, I still have no idea whether the project resulted in a 'technological advance'."
Deficiencies in Contemporaneous Documentation and the Burden of Proof

The fifth criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic framework examines whether the taxpayer maintained a detailed contemporaneous record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed. While the Income Tax Act does not prescribe a mandatory statutory template for technical records, Canadian tax courts consistently treat contemporaneous documentation as the primary evidentiary vehicle for proving that systematic experimentation actually occurred during the taxation years in issue.

In Dave's Diesel, the Appellant relied on handwritten diaries for 2013 and 2014 (Exhibits A-3 and A-4) that Mr. Dave said he wrote at the end of each day on which SR&ED work was done, most of whose entries the Court described as rather concise, together with a partial record of a single test performed on a C7 injector in each of 2013 and 2014 (Exhibits A-2 and A-1). These notebooks functioned as casual shop logs noting when parts arrived from a machine shop or when a component broke during handling, rather than structured engineering lab books. They contained no pre-test hypothesis statements, no test matrices, no dimensional tolerances, no hydraulic pressure logs, and no analytical conclusions linking test failures to subsequent design modifications. The Court expressly held that the two partial test records were insufficient and that the lack of documentation made it almost impossible for the Appellant to meet its onus on the second and third Northwest Hydraulic criteria; even combined with the physical presentation of six fuel injectors at trial (Exhibits AP-1 to AP-6), this evidence fell far short of discharging the Appellant's civil burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen against the legal standard of proof articulated by the Tax Court of Canada, the Appellant's specific evidentiary and technical failures, and the resulting judicial determination.

headers: Taxpayer's Factual & Evidentiary Failure in Dave's Diesel

cells: 1. Technological Risk or Uncertainty
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 1); Logix Data Products Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 36, at paragraph 69)

Objective "Competent Professional" Standard: Uncertainty must exist at the level of the industry state of the art such that a qualified professional in the field (e.g., a mechanical engineer) could not resolve the problem using routine engineering or standard procedures. Subjective ignorance of untrained workers is legally irrelevant.

Project team consisted of a General Manager with a business/marketing background, his father, and two unskilled labourers; none of the individuals involved were engineers or mechanics. Team disassembled injectors simply to learn how they functioned. No evidence was led to show a mechanical engineer could not rebuild the injectors using standard procedures.

Failed. The Court held that if the standard were subjective, "a grade school student trying to build a simple electric motor would meet the test". Subjective lack of knowledge does not create technological uncertainty.
2. Formulation of Hypotheses

Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2); Justice Sommerfeldt in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), citing Advanced Agricultural Testing Inc. v. The Queen (2009 TCC 190)

Discrete, Falsifiable Statements: A hypothesis is "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial". Claimants must formulate discrete, predictive hypotheses prior to each specific test aimed at eliminating a specific technological uncertainty (e.g., "An O-ring 5 mm. thick should withstand pressure of 50 lb/ft. as effectively as an O-ring 7.5 mm. thick").

Witness testified that the technological uncertainty was "whether we could successfully develop a process to remanufacture the injector[s]" and that the hypothesis was "whether we could develop a remanufacturing procedure and be able to remanufacture these injectors". No discrete hypotheses were formulated prior to individual shim thickness, O-ring, or spring pressure tests.
Failed. Justice Spiro rejected the circular conflation of the overarching commercial goal with a hypothesis, noting that such an argument belongs in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
3. Accordance with the Scientific Method
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3); National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72)

Systematic Observation, Measurement, and Experiment: Must follow Bowman J.'s 5-stage process. Requires defined pass/fail standards, controlled variables, precise measurement of inputs (e.g., pressures, durations), quantitative recording of failure thresholds, and iterative modification of hypotheses.

Workers engaged in ad-hoc shop-floor "tinkering" and "simple trial and error" (testing without prior hypothesis formulation). For spring pressure and shim tests, there was no record of the shim thicknesses tested, the pass/fail standard, applied pressures, durations, test results, or failure points.

Failed. No evidence that any of the four individuals used established and objective principles of scientific method; even a cursory review of the diary entries suggested the project had more in common with "tinkering" or "simple trial and error" than with the scientific method.
4. Technological Advancement
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4)

Advancement of Technological Knowledge: The process must generate new technological knowledge or capability that advances the field beyond routine engineering, distinct from commercial profitability or ecological benefits.

Appellant sought a new source of income after manufacturers stopped paying it for warranty remanufacturing work, but did not remanufacture a single Delphi 4 Pin, C7, or ISX injector in 2013 or 2014, nor articulate any new technological knowledge gained.

Failed. The Court distinguished an "environmental advance" and a "financial advance" from a "technological advance," stating that, after hearing all the evidence, he still had no idea whether the project resulted in a technological advance.
5. Contemporaneous Detailed Record
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5); National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72)

Verifiable Progression of Experimentation: Contemporaneous records must document the logical progression from hypothesis formulation to test parameters, quantitative observations, analysis, and hypothesis modification as the work progresses.

Relied on brief, anecdotal handwritten diary entries (e.g., noting a broken O-ring upon installing a prototype adapter from a machine shop) and physical injector exhibits (AP-1 to AP-6) at trial, plus a partial record of a single C7 test in each of 2013 and 2014 (Exhibits A-2 and A-1). No systematic logs of hypotheses, test conditions, or quantitative results were kept.

Failed. The lack of documentation made it almost impossible to meet the onus on the second and third criteria; the partial records of a single test in each year were insufficient to discharge that onus.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers and their technical tax advisors can operationalize the judicial holdings of Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen, the following two applied industry case studies model projects that initially exhibit the exact legal and evidentiary vulnerabilities identified by Justice Spiro. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remedial restructuring across project governance, technical documentation, contractual frameworks, and experimentation tracking to satisfy subsection 248(1) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act.
Case Study 1: Heavy-Duty Diesel Powertrain Remanufacturing & High-Pressure Common Rail (HPCR) Injector Re-Engineering
Initial Project Posture and Inherent Legal Pitfalls

A mid-sized diesel component rebuilder in Mississauga, Ontario ("Ontario Diesel Corp." or "ODC") seeks to develop a remanufacturing process for proprietary Euro VI / EPA Tier 4 Final High-Pressure Common Rail (HPCR) piezoelectric fuel injectors operating at rail pressures of 2,500 bar (36,260 psi). Because the OEM refuses to release internal dimensional tolerances, piezo-stack actuator trim codes, or replacement control valve seats to independent rebuilders, ODC's shop floor supervisor and three unlicensed shop hands begin cutting open used injector cores on a lathe, measuring internal shims with hand calipers, ordering generic aftermarket O-rings and control valves from a local machine shop, and running the reassembled injectors on a test bench until they leak or seize. ODC records these efforts in a daily shop planner ("Tried thicker shim on Unit #4; leaked at high idle") and claims 100% of the shop wages and machine shop invoices as SR&ED under paragraph 248(1)(c).

Under Dave's Diesel, this claim faces certain disallowance by the CRA and dismissal by the Tax Court of Canada. First, the project suffers from the subjective uncertainty pitfall: unlicensed shop hands cutting open injectors to discover OEM dimensions are merely overcoming their own subjective lack of knowledge rather than addressing a gap in the technological state of the art. Second, the project claims ineligible reverse engineering, as disassembling existing commercial products to measure geometries and fabricating basic disassembly fixtures constitute routine mechanical engineering. Third, the workflow lacks discrete hypotheses and the scientific method, because swapping shims and O-rings without pre-formulated predictive statements or quantitative telemetry is "simple trial and error" under Justice Spiro's Footnote 17 definition.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance & Establishing the Competent Professional Baseline

To satisfy Justice Spiro's and Justice Monaghan's objective standard of technological uncertainty, ODC must immediately anchor its project governance in recognized professional engineering qualifications. ODC appoints a licensed Professional Engineer (P.Eng., Mechanical/Metallurgical Engineering) with expertise in high-pressure fluid dynamics and tribology as the Principal SR&ED Investigator, supported by certified Red Seal Heavy Duty Equipment Technicians (421A). Prior to commencing any SR&ED claim, the P.Eng. executes and documents a comprehensive baseline review of publicly available patents, SAE International technical papers, Bosch/Delphi hydraulic specifications, and standard tribological data. This baseline report explicitly establishes what a competent mechanical engineer can resolve via routine engineering—such as ultrasonic cleaning, standard coordinate measuring machine (CMM) reverse-engineering of housing threads, and static seal selection—versus where the public body of technological knowledge genuinely runs out.
Step 2: Segregating Routine Reverse Engineering from Objective Technological Uncertainty

ODC bifurcates its project accounting into two distinct cost centres: Phase A (Commercial Pre-Requisite / Routine Engineering, which is excluded from SR&ED) and Phase B (Experimental Development, which is claimed under paragraphs 248(1)(c) and (d)). Within Phase A, all activities involving tearing down the injector cores to learn how they work, mapping component geometries via CMM, and fabricating disassembly wrenches (mirroring Steps 1 and 2 of the Dave's Diesel process) are strictly segregated and excluded from the Form T661 claim.

Within Phase B, through the P.Eng.'s baseline analysis, ODC isolates a genuine, objective technological uncertainty that a competent mechanical engineer cannot resolve using standard textbooks or routine engineering. Specifically, when salvaging fatigued OEM AISI 52100 bearing-steel control valve seats in 2,500 bar piezoelectric injectors via precision micro-lapping (5 μm material removal), the removal of the factory case-hardened layer induces localized cavitation erosion and micro-elastic seat deformation under high-frequency (5 kHz) multi-injection pulsing. It is technologically uncertain whether a thin-film Physical Vapour Deposition (PVD) Tungsten Disulfide (WS<sub>2</sub>) / Diamond-Like Carbon (DLC) duplex coating can restore hydrodynamic sealing integrity without altering the hydraulic armature lift response delay beyond the ±12 μs deterministic threshold required by the engine control unit (ECU).
Step 3: Formulating Discrete, Quantitative Hypotheses & Experimental Protocols

Replacing the circular Alice's Adventures in Wonderland goal statement condemned by Justice Spiro ("Can we remanufacture this injector?"), the P.Eng. institutes a mandatory Pre-Test Hypothesis Authorization Protocol. No bench test may be executed without a signed, date-stamped hypothesis sheet that directly mirrors Justice Spiro's O-ring benchmark example and answers every quantitative question posed in the Dave's Diesel judgment.

In Iteration H-1.1, the team formulates a discrete hypothesis statement prior to testing: "Applying a 2.5 μm PVD DLC coating over a 0.5 μm chromium interlayer on a micro-lapped AISI 52100 control valve seat, paired with an armature shim preload of 42.0 N ± 0.5 N, will withstand continuous cyclic rail pressure of 2,500 bar at 5 kHz actuation for 100 hours while restricting static return back-leakage to < 20.0 mm3/stroke and maintaining hydraulic injection delay within 115 μs ± 12 μs." The protocol establishes strict controlled variables and pass/fail standards, holding rail pressure constant at 2,500 bar ± 25 bar with ISO 4113 calibration oil maintained at 40°C ± 1°C for a target duration of 100.0 hours (1.8 × 109 cycles), where passing requires zero spallation under 500× scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and back-leakage < 20.0 mm3/stroke.

During empirical measurement and failure analysis, at hour 34.2 (6.15 × 10<sup>8</sup> cycles), back-leakage spikes to 47.8 mm<sup>3</sup>/stroke and the test is terminated. Profilometry and SEM reveal cohesive delamination of the DLC layer at the 60° conical seat interface due to Hertzian contact stress exceeding 3.2 GPa combined with fluid cavitation. In accordance with the scientific method, this failure drives a documented hypothesis modification for Iteration H-1.2, wherein the hypothesis is reformulated to test a graded silicon-doped DLC (Si-DLC) coating of 1.8 μm thickness combined with a modified seat cone angle of 61.5° to redistribute Hertzian contact stress below 2.4 GPa.
Step 4: Contractual Governance and Subcontractor Structuring

In Dave's Diesel, the Appellant ordered prototype adapters from an external machine shop. To ensure machine shop and PVD coating vendor costs qualify as eligible Canadian SR&ED subcontractor expenditures under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Act, ODC restructures its procurement contracts. The Statement of Work (SOW) with the Canadian machine shop and PVD coating vendor explicitly states that the fabrication work is performed "on behalf of ODC" and is "commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of" ODC's experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(d), specifying the exact experimental coating thicknesses and cone angles tied to Hypotheses H-1.1 and H-1.2. Furthermore, ODC retains 100% ownership of all resulting foreground intellectual property, experimental geometries, and process parameters, and compensates the subcontractor on a time-and-materials basis regardless of whether the prototype coatings fail during testing. Any components subsequently fabricated for commercial resale are contracted under separate commercial purchase orders and excluded from the SR&ED claim, ensuring no contamination of experimental prototype expenditures.
Step 5: Contemporaneous Documentation Architecture

To satisfy the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion and avoid the record-keeping deficiencies identified by Justice Rennie in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) (records not reflecting a logical progression between the premise of an experiment and the result), ODC replaces handwritten notebooks with a digital Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) integrated with its Bosch EPS test bench telemetry. Every experimental run generates an immutable, time-stamped record linking the pre-test hypothesis, exact pressure and duration profiles, raw sensor CSV exports, post-test failure microscopy, and the P.Eng.'s analytical conclusion driving the next hypothesis.

body.text: Case Study 2: Legacy Industrial Control System Modernization & Firmware Protocol Translation in Precision Manufacturing
Initial Project Posture and Inherent Legal Pitfalls

An industrial automation integrator in Waterloo, Ontario ("Waterloo Controls Inc." or "WCI") is contracted by a Tier-1 automotive stamping plant to replace obsolete 1990s proprietary Japanese programmable logic controllers (PLCs) on high-speed progressive die presses without replacing the legacy servo-hydraulic actuators and proprietary serial fieldbus backplanes. The OEM refuses to provide documentation on the proprietary fieldbus communication protocol or the closed-loop hydraulic damping algorithms.

WCI assigns two recent business-information-systems graduates (with no electrical engineering, computer engineering, or control systems credentials) to hook up a logic analyzer to the press wiring harness, trigger press strokes, guess what the hexadecimal data packets mean ("black-box probing"), and write Python scripts to mimic the packets. When the press experiences violent hydraulic chatter during high-speed stamping, the technicians randomly adjust proportional-integral-derivative (PID) gain numbers in the code until the vibration diminishes. WCI claims the entire customer contract cost as SR&ED, arguing that "figuring out how the undocumented legacy protocol works and making a new controller run the press without breaking it" is a technological uncertainty and a technological advance.

Under the legal principles established in Dave's Diesel, WCI's claim suffers from multiple disqualifying defects. First, WCI's black-box packet sniffing is merely routine reverse engineering to uncover existing, deterministic OEM design parameters, analogous to how Dave's Diesel took apart fuel injectors simply because it "did not understand how the injectors worked". Second, assigning business-IT graduates to tune high-speed servo-hydraulic control loops mirrors the Appellant's reliance on a General Manager who had studied business and marketing, his father, and two unskilled labourers, failing the objective competent professional test because a qualified control systems engineer could apply standard Ziegler-Nichols or Bode plot frequency-response methods to tune a conventional PID loop. Third, randomly guessing PID gain values without mathematical modelling or prior hypothesis formulation constitutes "simple trial and error". Fourth, because WCI is performing this work under a commercial contract for a Canadian manufacturing client, payments received from the client risk being classified as assistance or contract payments as defined in subsection 127(9) of the Act, which under subsection 127(18) reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures before ITCs are calculated.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Establishing Professional Competence & Segregating Routine Protocol Decoding

WCI restructures its technical team by placing the project under the direct technical supervision of a licensed Computer/Electrical Engineer (P.Eng.) specializing in real-time embedded control systems and digital signal processing (DSP). WCI immediately isolates all hours spent probing the legacy serial bus, mapping hexadecimal register addresses, and translating instruction sets into a non-SR&ED commercial work package. The P.Eng. documents that protocol decoding—however tedious—does not advance computer science or electrical engineering knowledge, as the underlying protocol already exists in the OEM hardware.

Once the protocol is mapped, the P.Eng. conducts a formal timing and frequency-domain analysis and identifies an objective system uncertainty. Specifically, when bridging a modern 32-bit ARM Cortex-R5 real-time microcontroller (operating on a 1 GHz asynchronous clock domain) to the legacy 500 kbps half-duplex RS-485 current-loop actuator backplane, deterministic bus arbitration collisions and electromagnetic interference (EMI) from 400 A solenoid switching induce variable packet-frame jitter of 85 μs to 420 μs. Standard IEEE 1588 precision time protocol (PTP) and conventional PID control algorithms fail because the hydraulic servo-valves require deterministic position-loop updates within a strict ±15 μs phase margin to prevent harmonic resonance in the press ram at 180 strokes/minute. It is technologically uncertain whether a predictive state-estimator embedded within a custom Direct Memory Access (DMA) interrupt service routine can compensate for stochastic physical-layer bus jitter while maintaining worst-case execution time (WCET) below 12 μs on memory-constrained hardware.
Step 2: Formulating Iterative Hypotheses & Eliminating Trial-and-Error Debugging

WCI prohibits unrecorded "code tweaking" on the shop floor. Instead, the P.Eng. structures the investigation around the five-stage Northwest Hydraulic scientific method. Prior to writing experimental code for Iteration H-2.1, the team records a discrete, falsifiable hypothesis: "Implementing a fixed-point Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) state-predictor inside the L1-cache-locked DMA interrupt handler, utilizing a 3rd-order autoregressive jitter model, will bound hydraulic valve actuation phase error to ≤ ±14.0 μs under injected 1.5 kV/m EMI burst noise while keeping CPU interrupt utilization below 18% at a 10 kHz sampling rate."

Rather than observing subjectively whether the press "chatters," WCI conducts methodical testing and metrology on a Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) test rig equipped with a 4-channel 1 GHz digital storage oscilloscope, an arbitrary waveform EMI noise generator, and hardware trace macrocells recording exact clock-cycle execution latency. Quantitative test logs demonstrate that while the 3rd-order EKF bounds phase error to ±11.2 μs, floating-point-to-fixed-point matrix inversion overflows the 12 μs WCET budget at 19.4 μs during peak EMI bursts, causing buffer underruns. The hypothesis is then systematically modified for Iteration H-2.2 to replace full matrix inversion with a Cholesky-decomposed square-root unscented filter combined with dynamic bit-shift quantization, successfully reducing WCET to 9.8 μs and generating quantifiable technological advancement in hard real-time state estimation.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring to Mitigate subsection 127(18) Assistance and Contract Payment Reductions

To ensure WCI's qualified expenditures are not eroded by the assistance or contract payment rules under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the Income Tax Act, WCI's tax counsel redrafts the commercial agreement with the automotive stamping client prior to project commencement. The agreement is structured strictly as a fixed-price commercial contract for the sale of a physical hardware product (a retrofitted PLC hardware appliance with a standard performance warranty), rather than a service contract to perform SR&ED on behalf of the customer. Furthermore, the contract explicitly stipulates that WCI undertakes all underlying research and engineering on its own account and at its sole financial risk, retains 100% legal and beneficial ownership of all firmware architectures, algorithms, and patents developed, and grants the customer only a non-exclusive licence to use the compiled binary firmware embedded within the delivered appliance. This contractual allocation of risk and intellectual property insulates WCI's eligible SR&ED expenditure pool from reduction under subsection 127(18).
Step 4: Contemporaneous Evidence Integration

WCI configures its Git version-control repository and Jira engineering ticketing system to enforce SR&ED compliance contemporaneously as the work progresses. Every Git branch corresponding to an experimental iteration requires a mandatory commit template containing the Hypothesis ID, predicted WCET and jitter thresholds, links to oscilloscope waveform captures, and the post-test analytical post-mortem explaining why the code branch was merged or abandoned. This creates an unbroken, verifiable evidentiary chain linking experimental premise to empirical result.
Synthesis of Remedial Governance Across Both Case Studies

The table below synthesizes the operational transformation required to move from the non-compliant posture of Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen to an audit-defensible Canadian SR&ED claim across both mechanical and embedded systems domains.

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions for Canadian Tax Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen does not alter the statutory law governing SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act; rather, it sharpens the evidentiary teeth of the Northwest Hydraulic test in the wake of the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72). For Canadian tax counsel, technical advisors, and corporate claimants, three enduring legal principles emerge from Justice Spiro's reasons for judgment.

First, the Tax Court assesses technological uncertainty objectively, from the perspective of a competent professional in the field, and Justice Spiro emphasized that the Appellant called neither a mechanical engineer nor a duly qualified diesel engine mechanic on this critical question. While subsection 248(1) does not contain an explicit statutory requirement that a claimant employ licensed engineers or Ph.D. scientists, attempting to prove an objective technological uncertainty through the testimony of individuals lacking formal technical training creates an almost insurmountable evidentiary hurdle. Where an SME lacks in-house degreed engineers, retaining an external P.Eng. or qualified subject-matter expert during the project planning phase to validate that the technical obstacles transcend routine industry procedures is essential to surviving CRA technical review and Tax Court scrutiny.

Second, advisors preparing Form T661 technical narratives must ruthlessly eliminate teleological or goal-oriented phrasing from the articulation of technological uncertainties and hypotheses. Stating that the uncertainty or hypothesis was "whether the company could design, build, or remanufacture Product X to meet specification Y" invites immediate judicial rejection under Justice Spiro's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland critique. Every claimed project must be decomposed into a sequence of discrete, falsifiable hypotheses that explicitly state the independent technical variable being manipulated, the quantitative physical or computational mechanism being tested, and the measurable dependent threshold defining success or failure.

Finally, Dave's Diesel confirms that casual shop diaries, uncalibrated trial-and-error adjustments, and physical prototypes presented in a courtroom cannot substitute for systematic, contemporaneous experimental records. To discharge the civil burden of proof on a balance of probabilities, contemporaneous documentation must explicitly answer the foundational metrological questions posed by Justice Spiro: the exact baseline standard selected for passing the test, the precise magnitude and duration of the experimental inputs applied, the quantitative measurements recorded at each interval, the exact threshold at which failure occurred, and the logical modification of the hypothesis that governed the subsequent experimental trial.
